Slide 1 of 72 · D1 — C# Core
C# Type System
What this primarily describes: Value types are mostly simple/primitive data (int, bool, DateTime, small structs) stored directly in the variable (the bits live with the variable). Reference types (class, string, List<T>) are more complex objects on the heap — the variable stores the starting address (an arrow) to that object, so two variables can share one object.

Definition

In C#, a variable does not always “hold the object.” Value types (simple/primitive data like int, bool, DateTime, small structs) store their bits directly in the variable. Reference types (class DTOs, string, List<T>) store the starting address (an arrow) of a heap object — so two variables can point at the same box.
  • Value types: int, bool, DateTime, struct — assignment copies the bits (independent copies).
  • Reference types: class DTOs, string, List<T> — assignment copies the address/reference (same object).
  • Boxing: putting a value into object (or untyped SQL param) allocates on the heap — avoid on busy schedule/payment APIs.
  • struct vs class: small immutable value → struct; shared mutable appointment/patient DTO across layers → class.

Picture — where the data lives

Value types keep the bits in the variable. Reference types keep a pointer; the object is on the heap.

Value type — int a = 10

STACK / inline
┌─────────────┐
│ a │ 10 │ ← value lives here
└─────────────┘
┌─────────────┐
│ b │ 10 │ ← copy of 10
└─────────────┘
b = 99 → only b changes
vs

Reference type — var r = new[]{1,2}

STACK        HEAP
┌──────┐     ┌──────────┐
│ r1 ●─┼───────▶│ [1, 2] │
└──────┘     └──────────┘
┌──────┐           ▲
│ r2 ●─┼───────────────┘ same object
└──────┘
r2[0]=99 → r1 also sees 99

One-line memory: value = copy the number · reference = copy the arrow (both arrows can point at one box).

Quick pick (project)

Use value / struct when…

  • Small fixed data (Point, Money)
  • Copying is OK / wanted
  • No shared mutation across layers
vs

Use class when…

  • DTO shared Controller → DA → Ok()
  • Nullability + mutable fields
  • Appointment / patient identity

My project: class DTOs + typed SqlParameter (avoid boxing).

Boxing in one glance

→

Boxing allocates. Prefer List<int> over old ArrayList of ints.

Step-by-step (beginner friendly)

  • Step 1 — Value vs reference (with before/after)

    A value type variable holds the bits. A reference type holds an arrow to one heap object — two variables can share the same DTO/list.

    ❌ Value type
    int a = 10; int b = a; // COPY value b = 99; // a is still 10
    ✔ Reference type
    var list1 = new List<int> { 1, 2 }; var list2 = list1; // COPY arrow list2.Add(3); // list1.Count is 3 — same list
    # INPUT
    int a = 10; int b = a; b = 99; Console.WriteLine(a); // 10 var list1 = new List<int> { 1, 2 }; var list2 = list1; list2.Add(3); Console.WriteLine(list1.Count); // 3
    # OUTPUT (same line as each WriteLine)
    10 3

    Takeaway: value = copy the number · reference = copy the arrow.

  • Step 2 — Boxing on SQL parameters (before/after)

    Boxing = store a value type inside object on the heap (allocates). On hot API paths we avoid the untyped parameter API.

    ❌ Before
    // BEFORE — Add takes object → boxes int int patientId = 42; cmd.Parameters.Add("@PatientId", patientId); // int → object (heap alloc every call)
    ✔ After
    // AFTER — typed SqlParameter + SqlDbType int patientId = 42; cmd.Parameters.Add( new SqlParameter("@PatientId", SqlDbType.Int) { Value = patientId }); // SQL type declared as Int up front
    How this avoids the boxing problem
    1. Trigger: anytime an int must become object, the CLR boxes it (heap copy).
    2. Before: Add(name, patientId) expects object → patientId is boxed on every SQL call in schedule/payment DA.
    3. After: build SqlParameter(..., SqlDbType.Int) first. You tell ADO.NET “this is SQL Int,” instead of handing a bare object into the collection.
    4. Why it matters: less GC pressure on busy APIs + correct SQL type (no AddWithValue guessing).
    BEFORE: int ──box──▶ object ──▶ Add(name, object) AFTER: int ──▶ SqlParameter(SqlDbType.Int) ──▶ SQL INT
    # INPUT
    int n = 42; object boxed = n; // boxing int back = (int)boxed; // unboxing Console.WriteLine(back);
    # OUTPUT (same line as each WriteLine)
    42

    Project line: typed SqlDbType on schedule/payment parameter binding = avoid object-add boxing on the hot path.

  • Step 3 — struct vs class for DTOs (before/after)

    Use class when the same appointment/patient object is passed and updated across Controller → DA → API response. Use struct only for small immutable values.

    ❌ Before
    public struct ScheduleAppointmentDto { ... } // each layer gets a COPY
    ✔ After
    public class ScheduleAppointmentDto { public int AppointmentId { get; set; } public string PatientName { get; set; } } // shared instance across layers
    # INPUT
    readonly struct Money { public decimal Amount { get; } public string Currency { get; } public Money(decimal amount, string currency) => (Amount, Currency) = (amount, currency); } var fee = new Money(9.99m, "USD"); var copy = fee; Console.WriteLine(copy.Amount); class Order { public int Id { get; set; } } var o1 = new Order { Id = 1 }; var o2 = o1; o2.Id = 99; Console.WriteLine(o1.Id); // 99
    # OUTPUT (same line as each WriteLine)
    9.99 99

    Takeaway: DTO across layers → class; tiny immutable value → struct.

  • Step 4 — Nullable value types (before/after)

    Optional SQL columns should use int? / DateTime?, not magic zeros or MinValue.

    ❌ Before
    DateTime end = DateTime.MinValue; // “missing?”
    ✔ After
    DateTime? end = reader["EndTime"] as DateTime?; if (end is null) { /* missing */ }

    Takeaway: ? on value types = true missing without a reference type.

KindExamples in my APIAssignment does…

ReferenceScheduleAppointmentDto, string, List<T>Copies the arrow (same object)

1. Value vs reference — full example

What it means: a value-type variable is the data. A reference-type variable holds a pointer to one heap object — so two names can share one DTO.

Why it matters in my project: Controller, DA, and API response all touch the same ScheduleAppointmentDto instance. If it were a struct, each layer would get a copy and updates would not travel together.

❌ Before
// BEFORE — think “= always copies data” var a = new List<int> { 1 }; var b = a; // looks like a copy… b.Add(2); // surprise: a also has 2 items Console.WriteLine(a.Count); // 2
✔ After
// AFTER — know reference shares the object var a = new List<int> { 1 }; var b = new List<int>(a); // real copy b.Add(2); Console.WriteLine(a.Count); // 1 Console.WriteLine(b.Count); // 2

Takeaway: value = copy the number · reference = copy the arrow.

2. Boxing — full example (SqlParameter)

What it means: boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap (allocation + copy). Unboxing casts it back.

Why it matters in my project: if you pass int/DateTime as plain object into SQL parameters, .NET boxes them on every call. On busy schedule/payment APIs that is extra GC pressure. Typed SqlParameter + SqlDbType is the fix we use in DA.

❌ Before
// BEFORE — API takes object → boxes the int int patientId = 42; cmd.Parameters.Add("@PatientId", patientId); // Add(string, object) → int becomes object (heap)
✔ After
// AFTER — typed SqlParameter + SqlDbType int patientId = 42; cmd.Parameters.Add( new SqlParameter("@PatientId", SqlDbType.Int) { Value = patientId }); // SQL type is Int — not a bare object bag
How typed SqlParameter avoids the boxing trap
  1. Boxing trigger: a value type (int, DateTime) must live inside something typed as object → CLR allocates a heap box and copies the bits.
  2. Before (bad path): Parameters.Add("@PatientId", patientId) uses an overload that takes object. Your int is therefore boxed on every call before it even reaches SQL.
  3. After (good path): create the parameter with an explicit SQL type first — new SqlParameter("@PatientId", SqlDbType.Int). ADO.NET already knows “this is an Int column,” so you are not stuffing a mystery object into the collection.
  4. What you gain: no untyped object-add boxing on the hot DA path; correct SQL type (Int / DateTime) instead of AddWithValue guessing; less GC pressure on busy schedule/payment APIs.
  5. Same idea elsewhere: prefer List<int> over List<object> — generics keep the value as int and never box.

Picture of the call:

BEFORE: int patientId ──box──▶ object ──▶ Parameters.Add(name, object) AFTER: int patientId ──▶ SqlParameter(SqlDbType.Int) ──▶ SQL INT (typed)

Level-3 line: “I avoid boxing on SqlParameter hot paths by using SqlDbType — I never pass int/DateTime as plain object into Add.”

3. struct vs class — full example (DTO choice)

What it means: struct = value semantics (copied). class = reference semantics (shared identity, mutation, inheritance).

Why it matters in my project: appointments/patients are mapped from SqlDataReader into class DTOs — mutated and passed across Controller → DA → API response. A struct would copy at each hop and break shared updates / nullability patterns.

❌ Before
// BEFORE — struct DTO (wrong for shared mutation) public struct ScheduleAppointmentDto { public int AppointmentId { get; set; } public string PatientName { get; set; } } // each layer gets a COPY — updates may not stick
✔ After
// AFTER — class DTO (correct for our layers) public class ScheduleAppointmentDto { public int AppointmentId { get; set; } public string PatientName { get; set; } } // same instance shared Controller → DA → Ok(dto)
ChooseWhenProject example
classShared mutation, nullability, across layersScheduleAppointmentDto
structSmall immutable value, copy is OKPoint, Money amount

4. Nullable value types — short example

What it means: int? / DateTime? can be “no value” without using a reference type. Useful for optional SQL columns (appointment end time may be null).

❌ Before
// BEFORE — magic 0 / MinValue as “missing” DateTime end = DateTime.MinValue; if (end == DateTime.MinValue) { /* missing? */ }
✔ After
// AFTER — nullable value type DateTime? end = reader["EndTime"] as DateTime?; if (end is null) { /* truly missing */ } else { Use(end.Value); }

Q2. How do you avoid boxing int patientId into a SQL parameter?
Show answer
Use typed SqlParameter("@PatientId", SqlDbType.Int) { Value = patientId } — not an untyped object add.
Q3. Why not make ScheduleAppointmentDto a struct?
Show answer
It is mutated and shared across layers. A struct would copy at each hop — updates would not travel together. Prefer class for identity / shared mutation.

My project story (from MyDotnet.md)

My project (D01): C# type system: value vs reference types, boxing, structs vs classes

How: In API Data Access, SqlParameter values and DTO properties mix value types (`int`, `DateTime`) and reference types (`string`, `List<>`). Mapped `SqlDataReader` columns into classes (reference) rather than structs because appointments/patients are mutated and passed across layers.

Why: Avoid unnecessary boxing when binding parameters; keep DTOs as classes for nullability and shared mutation in schedule/payment flows.

// value type param — no boxing when typed correctly new SqlParameter("@PatientId", SqlDbType.Int) { Value = patientId }; // reference type DTO shared across controller → DA → API response public class ScheduleAppointmentDto { public int AppointmentId { get; set; } public string PatientName { get; set; } }

Self rating: 3 (Expected TA: 3)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: show where boxing or struct vs class affected performance.
  • In my project API Data Access layer, I read data using SqlDataReader from stored procedures.
  • I map each row into a class DTO (Data Transfer Object) — reference type — for appointments and patients.
  • I use class instead of struct because the same object is passed and updated across Controller → DA (Data Access) → API response.
  • For SQL parameters, I use typed SqlParameter (SqlDbType.Int, SqlDbType.DateTime).
  • If I pass int/DateTime as plain object, .NET boxes them — extra memory allocation on busy schedule/payment APIs.
  • Example: new SqlParameter("@PatientId", SqlDbType.Int) { Value = patientId };
  • Result: less boxing overhead and stable shared DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) in production code.
Interview — questions & answers

Q: Where did boxing or struct vs class matter in your project?

A: Typed SqlParameter (SqlDbType.Int/DateTime) avoids boxing ints/dates as object on busy APIs. Appointment/patient DTOs are class because they are mutated and shared across layers — a struct would copy and break shared updates.

Q: What is boxing?

A: Converting a value type to object (or an interface) — allocates on the heap and copies the value. Prefer generics and typed parameters.

Q: When would you choose struct over class?

A: Small immutable value semantics (Point, Money) with no shared mutation. For DTOs across Controller → DA → response, use class.

Practice

  • Show typed SqlParameter vs boxing into object
  • Defend class DTO vs struct for appointments/patients across layers
  • Use DateTime? for an optional SQL column instead of MinValue

Slide 2 of 72 · D1 — C# Core
LINQ Execution Internals
What this primarily describes: LINQ means Language Integrated Query — a C# way to query collections (and databases via providers) with a style similar to writing a query script in SQL (Where/Select/OrderBy ≈ filter/project/sort). This slide primarily describes when that query actually runs (deferred execution) and the difference between in-memory IEnumerable and provider IQueryable.

Definition

A query looked frozen in time, but every enumeration reran it against changed data because LINQ had stored a recipe, not results. Remember: LINQ = Language Integrated Query — C# query syntax for collections/SQL-like filters.
  • Deferred: Most LINQ operators execute when the sequence is enumerated, not when the query is declared.
  • IEnumerable: Runs .NET delegates in the process over objects the application can enumerate.
  • IQueryable: Builds an expression tree that a provider translates, often into SQL.
  • Materialize: Use ToList() deliberately when a stable snapshot or single execution is required.

Step-by-step (beginner friendly)

  • Step 1 — Deferred (before/after)

    What it means: Most LINQ operators execute when the sequence is enumerated, not when the query is declared.

    ❌ Before
    // BEFORE — without the project fix // Risk: Materialize with `.ToList()` after mapping so multiple consumers (grid + report logic) don’t re-enumerate a closed reader or change mid-loop // definition-only / wrong pattern
    ✔ After
    var appointments = MapFromReader(dr).Where(a => a.Status != "Cancelled").ToList(); // force now // later safe: count + foreach both use same materialized list
    How this maps to my project
    1. How: Used LINQ-to-Objects on in-memory lists after ADO.NET reads (my project uses ADO.NET + SPs, not EF IQueryable). Hit deferred-execution bugs when enumerating filtered appointment lists twice after reader was closed.
    2. Why: Materialize with `.ToList()` after mapping so multiple consumers (grid + report logic) don’t re-enumerate a closed reader or change mid-loop.
    3. After code: use the green box / MyDotnet snippet.

    Takeaway: Deferred — pair the definition with Before → After.

  • Step 2 — IEnumerable (before/after)

    What it means: Runs .NET delegates in the process over objects the application can enumerate.

    ❌ Before
    // BEFORE — skip IEnumerable
    ✔ After
    // AFTER — apply IEnumerable with a project example

My project story (from MyDotnet.md)

My project (D02): LINQ internals: deferred execution, IEnumerable vs IQueryable

How: Used LINQ-to-Objects on in-memory lists after ADO.NET reads (my project uses ADO.NET + SPs, not EF IQueryable). Hit deferred-execution bugs when enumerating filtered appointment lists twice after reader was closed.

Why: Materialize with `.ToList()` after mapping so multiple consumers (grid + report logic) don’t re-enumerate a closed reader or change mid-loop.

var appointments = MapFromReader(dr).Where(a => a.Status != "Cancelled").ToList(); // force now // later safe: count + foreach both use same materialized list

Self rating: 3 (Expected TA: 3)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: explain a bug from deferred execution or multiple enumeration.
  • My project uses ADO.NET + stored procedures. After reading SQL, I use LINQ on in-memory lists (not EF (Entity Framework) IQueryable).
  • LINQ Where/Select is deferred — it does not run until you foreach, Count, or ToList.
  • Bug I hit: I filtered appointments with Where, then used the list twice after SqlDataReader was already closed.
  • Second use tried to run the deferred query again and failed or returned wrong/empty data.
  • Fix: call ToList() right after Where/Select to save results in memory once.
  • Result: controller and report logic both use the same safe snapshot.

Previous-project depth (if asked)

  • In my previous EF Core (Entity Framework Core) project, IQueryable deferred execution caused a similar bug.
  • Bug: built a query, disposed DbContext, then enumerated later — ObjectDisposedException.
  • Also: Count() + foreach on same IQueryable ran SQL twice (multiple enumeration).
  • Fix: ToList() while context was open; reuse the list afterward.
  • Result: same deferred-execution lesson with true IQueryable, not only in-memory LINQ.

Generics and Variance
What this primarily describes: Generics use a type placeholder such as T, so one type-safe design can work with many data types without casting — like a reusable container whose label says what it may hold. This slide focuses on variance (in/out): when a more specific type can safely be used where a more general type is expected, and when it cannot.

Definition

A report API could return dogs as animals without copying because its producer contract was safely marked out.
  • Generics: Provide compile-time type safety and reusable algorithms without routine casts.
  • out: Covariance permits a producer such as IEnumerable where IEnumerable is expected.
  • in: Contravariance permits a consumer of a broader type where a narrower consumer is expected.
  • Invariant: Mutable types such as List stay invariant because both reading and writing T must be safe.

  • Why: shared library needed one list/save contract across modules without unsafe casting.
  • Result: cleaner DI (Dependency Injection) registration and fewer cast bugs across services.

Slide 4 of 72 · D1 — C# Core
Exception Handling Strategy
What this primarily describes: An exception is .NET's signal that an operation failed unexpectedly, much like a database error that interrupts a SQL command. This slide focuses on an exception strategy: catching and logging errors, mapping them to safe API responses, and handling them globally with middleware so clients never see raw SQL or stack traces.

Definition

A failed order should become one consistent API error at the boundary, while its original stack remains available to operations.
  • Throw: Use exceptions for exceptional failures, not ordinary branching or validation flow.
  • Custom type: Add a domain exception when callers need stable semantic meaning or structured data.
  • Global handler: Map known exceptions to controlled responses and log unexpected failures once.
  • Rethrow: Use bare throw; to preserve the original stack trace.

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: explain our exception strategy including global handling.
  • At controller level: try/catch, log full error with ILogger, return safe HTTP message to client.

  • Global level: JWT (JSON Web Token) authentication failures are handled in middleware before controller runs.
  • Integration receivers: catch exception, log it, continue processing — one bad message must not stop the whole host.
  • Result: users see safe errors; developers see full details only in server logs.

Slide 5 of 72 · D1 — C# Core
CLR Memory Management
What this primarily describes: CLR means Common Language Runtime — the .NET engine that runs code and manages memory. GC means Garbage Collection, which reclaims unused managed objects, while IDisposable/using closes limited resources explicitly. This slide focuses on allocations and on preventing leaks such as undisposed SQL connections or readers that create pool pressure.

Definition

Memory kept climbing after traffic fell, so the team separated allocation rate from retained objects and leaked native resources.
  • Generations: The GC promotes surviving objects; long-lived references can move objects into older generations.
  • LOH: Large allocations generally land on the Large Object Heap and can increase pause and fragmentation pressure.
  • IDisposable: Dispose deterministic resources promptly with using; GC timing is not resource cleanup.
  • Diagnosis: Use counters and dumps to distinguish high churn, rooted retention, and undisposed handles.

My project story (from MyDotnet.md)

My project (D05): CLR memory / IDisposable / GC

How: Always `using` on SqlConnection/SqlDataReader/`IDisposable` in DA. Large report/registry exports stream or page rather than holding huge graphs. Fixed connection leaks by disposing readers after mapping.

Why: Azure SQL connection pool exhaustion and LOH pressure from large appointment/report lists hurt multi-tenant sites.

using var dr = _customerDA.ExecuteReader("usp_GetScheduleAppointmentDto", parms); while (dr.Read()) appointments.Add(MapFromReader(dr)); // connection/reader disposed → returned to pool

Self rating: 3 (Expected TA: 4)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: real memory/resource issue, root cause, and how you verified the fix.
  • Issue: under many concurrent clinic users, we saw SQL timeout and connection pool pressure.
  • Root cause: undisposed SqlDataReader/SqlConnection in DA (Data Access) code — resource leak, not a GC (Garbage Collection) tuning issue.
  • Fix: always use using/dispose; map reader to list, then close reader before returning API response.
  • Also avoid holding large Registry/report JSON in memory after processing.
  • Verified: pool timeout errors reduced after dispose fixes; checked IIS (Internet Information Services) and SQL error logs.
  • Gap vs Level-4: I did not use dotnet-dump or GC generation analysis.

Previous-project depth (if asked)

  • In my previous project we had a memory leak suspicion on a long-running Windows service.
  • I used process memory counters and Visual Studio diagnostic tools to see retained objects after a job cycle.
  • Root cause: static list kept growing with processed IDs (retained references), not only undisposed resources.
  • Fix: clear/bound the collection after each batch; dispose streams properly.
  • Result: memory stopped climbing overnight — closer to Level-4 diagnosis than dispose-only fixes.

Slide 6 of 72 · D1 — C# Core
Async / Await
What this primarily describes: async/await let a method pause for I/O (input/output such as SQL, HTTP, or file access) without occupying a thread for the whole wait — like taking another customer's order while the kitchen cooks. This slide focuses on releasing the thread at await, resuming when the result is ready, and avoiding sync-over-async with .Result or .Wait().

Definition

By default a method is synchronous — it holds the thread until it finishes. Add the async keyword so the method can release the thread while waiting; when the result is ready, work resumes (often on a thread-pool thread).
  • Normal method: sync — thread stays busy until the method returns.
  • Make it async: put async on the method and use await where you wait (HTTP, DB, file).
  • Why: await frees the thread during the wait so other work can run; when the Task completes, the method continues after await.
  • Not a new OS thread per call — it is about not blocking while waiting.

Async Await Mechanics – Visual Guide

Flow to remember run → await (release thread) → result ready → resume after await release → complete → resume

async/await timeline (easy mental model)

1. Runmethod starts on a thread
→
2. awaitrelease the thread — wait for I/O
→
3. ReadyTask completes (result arrived)
→
4. Resumecontinue after await
↺

Not “new OS thread per call” — just don’t hold the thread while waiting.

Sync vs async at await

Sync (.Result / Sleep)

  • Thread sits idle while waiting
  • Other work cannot use that thread
  • Can deadlock under load
vs

async + await

  • Thread is free during the wait
  • Other requests can run
  • Resume when result is ready

Add the async keyword → use await → release → resume.

Step-by-step (beginner friendly)

  • Step 1 — Normal methods are sync
    By default a method is synchronous. The thread that calls it stays busy until the method returns — even if it is only waiting.
    # INPUT
    // SYNC — no async keyword; thread held while waiting string FetchSync() { Thread.Sleep(200); // blocks this thread return "sync-done"; } Console.WriteLine(FetchSync());
    # OUTPUT (same line as each WriteLine)
    sync-done

    Problem: while waiting, that thread cannot do other useful work.

  • Step 2 — Add async to make the method async
    To wait without blocking, add the async keyword and use await. Return type becomes Task / Task<T>.
    # INPUT
    // ASYNC — keyword async + await async Task FetchAsync() { await Task.Delay(200); // release thread while waiting return "async-done"; } Console.WriteLine(await FetchAsync());
    # OUTPUT (same line as each WriteLine)
    async-done
    PartMeaning
    asyncThis method may use await
    awaitWait here — but release the thread while waiting
    Task<string>Promise of a string later
  • Step 3 — Release thread → result ready → resume
    That is the whole point of async/await:
    1. Method runs until it hits await.
    2. Release: thread is free while I/O / delay runs.
    3. Result ready: Task completes.
    4. Resume: continue after await.
    # INPUT
    Console.WriteLine("1 before await"); await Task.Delay(50); Console.WriteLine("2 after resume");
    # OUTPUT (same line as each WriteLine)
    1 before await 2 after resume

    Remember: async does not mean “new OS thread per call.” It means “don’t hold the thread while waiting.”

  • Step 4 — Do not block with .Result / .Wait()
    If you mark a method async then block with .Result, you undo the benefit — and can deadlock.
    Bad — blocks again
    var data = FetchAsync().Result; // holds thread
    Good — await through
    var data = await FetchAsync(); // releases

Skill matrix D06 — start from basics: sync method → async keyword → release thread → resume.

Big picture

StepWhat happens
1. Sync method (default)Thread stays busy until the method finishes
2. Add asyncMethod may use await; return type is Task / Task<T>
3. Hit awaitRelease the thread while waiting for I/O
4. Result readyMethod resumes after await (takes a thread again)

Self-check quiz

Q1. Are methods async by default?
Show answer
No — methods are sync by default. You add the async keyword to allow await.
Q2. What does await do to the thread?
Show answer
It releases the thread while waiting. When the Task completes, the method continues after await.
Q3. Does async create a new OS thread every call?
Show answer
No — it is about not blocking while waiting, not spawning a thread per call.

My project story (from MyDotnet.md)

My project (D06): Async/await: state machine, sync-over-async, cancellation

How: Controllers and Wallet/outcomes/integration service calls are async. SignalR `Clients.Group(...).SendAsync`. Avoided `.Result`/`.Wait` on ASP.NET threads after seeing hangs during migration.

Why: Sync-over-async deadlocks under load; async keeps Kestrel threads free for schedule + payment APIs.

[HttpGet("GetAppointments")] public async Task<IActionResult> GetAppointments(...) { var results = await _scheduleService.GetAsync(patientId, from, to, ct); await _hubContext.Clients.Group(siteName).SendAsync("AppointmentUpdated", results, ct); return Ok(results); }

Self rating: 3 (Expected TA: 4)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: real async problem (blocking/cancellation) and how you fixed it.
  • Issue: some migrated API code used .Wait() or .Result on ASP.NET request threads.
  • Under load this blocked thread-pool threads and caused slow or hanging wallet/schedule APIs.
  • Fix: changed controllers to async Task<IActionResult> and used await for SQL, HttpClient, and payment calls.
  • I pass CancellationToken where supported so cancelled browser requests stop work sooner.
  • Result: API stays responsive during concurrent calls.
  • Gap: I have limited experience with custom timeout/circuit policies beyond basic async/await.
Interview — questions & answers

Q: How do you turn a sync method into async?

A: Add the async keyword, change the return type to Task / Task<T>, and await async APIs instead of blocking.

Q: What does async do to the thread?

A: At await, the method releases the thread while waiting. When the Task completes, execution resumes after the await.

Q: Why avoid .Result?

A: It blocks the thread again and can cause deadlocks or thread-pool starvation. Prefer await end-to-end.

Practice

  • Convert one sync method to async Task with await
  • Explain: release thread at await → resume when result ready
  • Find and remove one .Result / .Wait()

Slide 7 of 72 · D1 — C# Core
Threading and TPL
What this primarily describes: Concurrency means making progress on multiple operations during the same period; parallelism means actually running work at the same time on multiple CPU cores. TPL means Task Parallel Library, .NET's task-based toolkit for this work. This slide focuses on choosing Task/async for I/O waits, parallelism for CPU-bound work, and lock/Interlocked only when shared memory needs protection.

Definition

A counter lost updates even though every worker ran successfully; ++ was a read-modify-write race.
  • Task: Represents asynchronous work; use it for composition and thread-pool scheduling.
  • Thread: Use a dedicated thread only for requirements such as affinity or a long-lived blocking loop.
  • Parallel: Use bounded parallelism for independent CPU-bound work, not to make I/O artificially synchronous.
  • Interlocked: Use atomic operations for simple shared counters and lock for multi-step invariants.

  • I have not used Interlocked or Parallel.For for CPU-heavy work in this healthcare API project.

  • In my previous project a batch file import needed CPU work (parse + validate many rows).
  • I used Parallel.ForEach on independent rows with MaxDegreeOfParallelism limited to avoid overloading SQL.
  • For a shared counter of processed rows I used Interlocked.Increment instead of lock on every row.
  • Rule I follow: async Task for I/O; Parallel/Interlocked only for CPU-bound independent work.
  • Result: import finished faster without deadlocking the DB pool.

Channels and Backpressure
What this primarily describes: A producer/consumer flow separates the code that creates work from the code that processes it — like orders entering a kitchen queue for cooks to handle. This slide focuses on channels and queues, including backpressure that slows producers when consumers cannot keep up, preventing overload from exhausting memory.

Definition

When producers outran workers, an unbounded queue turned a traffic spike into an outage; a bounded channel made overload explicit.
  • Channel: Provides async producer/consumer coordination with single- or multi-reader/writer options.
  • Bounded: A bounded channel caps memory and defines whether writers wait, drop, or reject work.
  • Completion: Complete the writer and let readers drain; propagate terminal errors deliberately.
  • Concurrent collection: Choose a concurrent collection when its synchronous access pattern matches the workflow.

Delegates Events Expressions
What this primarily describes: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method, and an event notifies subscribers when something happens — similar to calling registered listeners. An expression tree stores code as inspectable data rather than immediately running it. This slide focuses on callbacks versus expression trees that EF/LINQ providers can translate into SQL.

Definition

The same lambda can be executable behavior or inspectable data: a delegate runs it, while an expression tree lets a provider translate it.
  • Delegate: A type-safe reference to executable method behavior.
  • Event: Restricts subscription and publication so only the declaring type raises notifications.
  • Expression: Expression<Func<T,bool>> represents code as a traversable tree.
  • Provider: IQueryable providers inspect expression trees and translate supported nodes into another language.

  • A normal Func/delegate would filter in memory after loading all rows (bad for large tables).
  • I also used C# events for "OrderSaved" to refresh UI after save.
  • Result: I understand when expression trees matter (EF/IQueryable) vs when compiled delegates run in process.

Reflection and Attributes
What this primarily describes: Reflection lets code inspect types, methods, and metadata at runtime; attributes are labels attached to code, like annotations on a form. This slide focuses on frameworks reading markers such as [Authorize] and [HttpGet] to drive routing, authorization, and tests.

Definition

A small attribute did nothing by itself; framework code used reflection to discover its metadata and apply behavior.
  • Attribute: Adds metadata to assemblies, types, members, or parameters.
  • Reflection: Reads type metadata and can inspect or invoke members dynamically.
  • Framework action: A scanner, filter provider, serializer, or DI component interprets discovered attributes.
  • Cost: Cache repeated metadata lookups and avoid unconstrained scanning on hot paths.

Slide 11 of 72 · D1 — C# Core
Allocation Aware C#
What this primarily describes: A hot path is code that runs very often or directly affects response time, so small costs there add up. Span<T> provides a lightweight view over contiguous memory and can avoid copies. This slide focuses on measuring with BenchmarkDotNet and reducing proven allocation bottlenecks instead of optimizing from guesses.

Definition

A parser became cheaper when it sliced existing buffers with Span<T> instead of creating a new string for every field.
  • Span: A stack-only view over contiguous memory, useful for synchronous parsing and slicing.
  • Memory: A heap-storable memory view suitable across asynchronous boundaries.
  • Allocation: Remove allocations only on measured hot paths; readability remains a design constraint.
  • Benchmark: Use representative data, warmup, multiple runs, and allocation diagnostics.

Modern .NET Migration
What this primarily describes: .NET Framework is the older Windows-focused runtime, while modern .NET is the current cross-platform platform. TFM means Target Framework Moniker, the label that declares which framework an app targets. This slide focuses on the real migration work across dependencies, hosting, authentication, and configuration, using phased delivery rather than only changing the TFM.

Definition

Changing the target framework was the smallest part of migration; unsupported libraries, configuration, authentication, and hosting carried the real risk.
  • Inventory: Map projects, APIs, NuGet packages, Windows-only dependencies, and deployment assumptions.
  • Modernize: Replace unsupported framework features and move configuration and hosting to modern patterns.
  • Validate: Test authentication, serialization, globalization, networking, and operational behavior.
  • Rollout: Use staged deployment, telemetry, and a rollback path rather than a big-bang switch.

  • I handled JWT (JSON Web Token) auth, IIS (Internet Information Services)/Kestrel hosting, package differences (Newtonsoft vs System.Text.Json), and phased endpoint moves.
  • Deployment: Azure DevOps build/publish to IIS plus SQL scripts deployed in same release window.
  • Why phased: big-bang rewrite would risk clinic downtime.

Slide 13 of 72 · D1 — C# Core
Runtime Diagnostics Tools
What this primarily describes: Runtime diagnostics are measurements captured while an application runs — traces show where time went, counters show changing totals, and dumps preserve process state for inspection. This slide focuses on using that evidence to prove why a production app is slow, hung, or leaking memory.

Definition

CPU was high but logs were quiet, so runtime counters narrowed the symptom and a trace revealed the hot call stacks.
  • Counters: Observe live rates and gauges such as CPU, allocation rate, GC, exceptions, and thread-pool state.
  • Trace: Capture time-based runtime events and stacks to locate expensive or blocked work.
  • Dump: Inspect a process snapshot for heaps, roots, threads, locks, and exception state.
  • Method: Start with a hypothesis, collect the least disruptive evidence, and compare before and after.

Slide 14 of 72 · D1 — C# Core
NuGet Dependency Resolution
What this primarily describes: NuGet is .NET's package manager, similar to pip for Python; a transitive dependency is a package brought in by another package. This slide focuses on diagnosing version conflicts and aligning direct and transitive package versions so builds and runtimes stay consistent.

Definition

A harmless package update changed a transitive version and broke runtime loading, so the team inspected the resolved graph, not just direct references.
  • Graph: Restore resolves direct and transitive package requirements into one dependency graph.
  • Conflict: Incompatible constraints or runtime assets can cause restore warnings, compile failures, or runtime errors.
  • Pin: A direct reference can intentionally constrain a transitive version, but ownership and upgrades must be documented.
  • Repeatability: Central versions and lock files can make dependency resolution more consistent.

Slide 15 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
ASP.NET Core Pipeline
What this primarily describes: The ASP.NET Core request pipeline is the ordered chain each HTTP request passes through, like checkpoints before reaching an endpoint. CORS means Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, the browser rule controlling calls between origins. This slide focuses on middleware order, routing, filters, authorization, CORS, and SignalR token handling from request to response.

Definition

Authorization appeared configured but never protected an endpoint because pipeline order placed it before routing had selected endpoint metadata.
  • Middleware: Runs in registration order on the way in and unwinds in reverse on the way out.
  • Routing: Matches an endpoint and exposes its metadata for later middleware.
  • Filters: Wrap MVC or endpoint execution at framework-specific stages, not the entire server pipeline.
  • Order: Exception handling, routing, authentication, authorization, and endpoints must be deliberately ordered.

My project (D15): ASP.NET Core pipeline: middleware order

How: Auth → SignalRAccessTokenMiddleware → SignalRCorsMiddleware → Routing → Controller (documented in API). Wrong order broke hub negotiate (token missing) or CORS preflight.

Self rating: 3 (Expected TA: 4)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: trace a request end-to-end and explain why middleware order mattered.
  • Real case: after Core migration, web client hub connection returned 401 Unauthorized.
  • End-to-end path: browser → IIS (Internet Information Services)/Kestrel → Authentication → token middleware → CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) → hub/controller → DA (Data Access) → SQL.
  • Problem: WebSocket sends JWT (JSON Web Token) in query string, not header. Auth ran before token was copied to header.
  • Correct order: Authentication → SignalRAccessTokenMiddleware → SignalRCorsMiddleware → endpoints.
  • Result: negotiate/connect works; order documented for the team.

Slide 16 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
DI Lifetimes and Captivity
What this primarily describes: DI means Dependency Injection — the framework creates and hands a class the services it needs instead of the class building them itself. Lifetimes say how long each service instance lives: singleton, scoped, or transient. This slide focuses on choosing lifetimes and avoiding a captive dependency, where a singleton incorrectly holds a scoped service.

Definition

A singleton worker captured a scoped DbContext, turning per-operation state into a long-lived object shared far beyond its intended boundary.
  • Transient: Creates an instance at each resolution; suitable for lightweight stateless services.
  • Scoped: Creates one instance per scope, commonly one web request or explicit background-work scope.
  • Singleton: Creates one application-wide instance and therefore requires thread-safe state and dependencies.
  • Captive: A longer-lived service must not directly retain a shorter-lived dependency.

Slide 17 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
Reliable Web API Contracts
What this primarily describes: A Web API contract is the agreed shape and behavior of requests and responses, like a typed agreement between client and server. API means Application Programming Interface. This slide focuses on model binding, validation, versioning, and consistent safe errors through status codes and ProblemDetails.

Definition

Clients stopped parsing one-off error shapes when every failure—validation, domain conflict, or server error—used one stable ProblemDetails contract.
  • Binding: Converts route, query, header, form, and body inputs into endpoint parameters or models.
  • Validation: Rejects invalid input at a clear boundary and returns field-level details where safe.
  • Versioning: Evolves contracts with an explicit compatibility and retirement policy.
  • ProblemDetails: Provides a standard machine-readable error shape with stable type and status semantics.

Slide 18 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
EF Core Query Behavior
What this primarily describes: EF Core means Entity Framework Core; it is an ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) that maps C# classes to SQL tables and turns LINQ into SQL. This slide focuses on tracking, loading related data, and avoiding N+1 queries, plus the equivalent ADO.NET and SP (stored procedure) patterns when EF is not used.

Definition

A page issued one order query and then one customer query per row; projection replaced the hidden N+1 round trips with one shaped query.
  • Tracking: Use tracking when entities will be changed and saved in the same unit of work.
  • No tracking: Use AsNoTracking for read-only results to reduce tracking overhead.
  • Loading: Choose projection, eager, explicit, or lazy loading with query count and payload in mind.
  • N+1: Detect repeated per-row queries through SQL logs or tracing and reshape the query.

My project (D18): EF Core: tracking, N+1, migrations

How: my project API uses **ADO.NET + stored procedures**, not EF Core. Equivalent issues: loops calling SP per row (chatty DA) — fixed by set-based SP or batch. Registry uses Cosmos DB SDK.

Why: Legacy performance and multi-tenant SQL patterns favor SPs.

using var dr = _customerDA.ExecuteReader("usp_GetScheduleAppointmentDto", parms); while (dr.Read()) appointments.Add(MapFromReader(dr)); // one round-trip

Self rating: 2 (Expected TA: 3)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: fix N+1 and explain tracking vs no-tracking.
  • Our API does not use EF Core (Entity Framework Core) — we use ADO.NET + stored procedures.
  • N+1 equivalent I fixed: DA (Data Access) loop calling SP (Stored Procedure) once per row for appointments.
  • Fix: one set-based stored procedure returns all rows in single round-trip.
  • No-tracking equivalent: read SqlDataReader, map to DTO (Data Transfer Object) list, close reader immediately — do not keep reader open.
  • Schema changes go through SQL scripts in repo, not EF migrations.

Previous-project depth (if asked)

  • In my previous project we used EF Core (Entity Framework Core) for order/list APIs.
  • Problem (N+1): loaded orders, then inside a loop called DB again for each order’s line items — many small queries, slow list page.
  • Fix: one query with Include (or projection Select) so orders + items come in fewer round-trips.
  • Tracking vs no-tracking: for read-only list screens I used AsNoTracking() so EF does not track entities (less memory, faster).
  • For update/save flows I kept tracking so SaveChanges() can detect changes.
  • Schema: team used EF migrations (Add-Migration / Update-Database) for table changes.

Q: Explain EF Core Query Behavior for an interviewer.

Q: What does Level-3 look like for this skill?

Q: Give your assessor talking points.

A: Level-3 asks: fix N+1 and explain tracking vs no-tracking. Our API does not use EF Core (Entity Framework Core) — we use ADO.NET + stored procedures. N+1 equivalent I fixed: DA (Data Access) loop calling SP (Stored Procedure) once per row for appointments. Fix: one set-based stored procedure returns all rows in single round-trip.

Slide 19 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
Authentication Flow Design
What this primarily describes: Authentication proves who a caller is; authorization decides what that caller may do. JWT means JSON Web Token — a signed pass an API checks on each request; OIDC means OpenID Connect, a standard identity layer for login. This slide focuses on Identity and bearer flows from login through token validation and expiry to protected APIs.

Definition

A JWT is not trusted because it can be decoded; the API trusts it only after validating its signature, issuer, audience, and lifetime.
  • Identity: ASP.NET Core Identity manages local users, credentials, tokens, and related account workflows.
  • OAuth2: Delegates authorization and access to protected resources through defined flows.
  • OIDC: Adds authentication and identity claims on top of OAuth 2.0.
  • Validation: Validate signature, issuer, audience, lifetime, and required authorization claims.

My project story (from MyDotnet.md)

My project (D19): Auth: Identity / JWT / OAuth2/OIDC

How: OIDC/JWT JWT bearer on API; `[Authorize]` on APIs; SignalR access token from query string middleware for hub connections.

Self rating: 2 (Expected TA: 3)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: draw auth flow end-to-end including token validation and expiry.
  • Flow: user logs in via OIDC (OpenID Connect)/JWT (JSON Web Token) provider → gets access token → sends token to API.
  • API uses JwtBearer middleware and [Authorize] on protected controllers.
  • If token expired or invalid → 401 → web client prompts re-login or refresh.
  • We do not use ASP.NET Identity membership database — central OIDC fits web client and WinForm.
  • Gap: I know API-side validation well; deep OIDC provider config is team-owned.

Previous-project depth (if asked)

  • In my previous project we used ASP.NET Identity for local users plus JWT (JSON Web Token) for API clients.
  • Flow: login → Identity checks password → issues JWT with claims → API validates signature/expiry on each call.
  • Refresh token endpoint issued new access token when short-lived JWT expired.
  • Roles/claims from Identity mapped into JWT for [Authorize(Roles=...)] checks.
  • Result: end-to-end auth I can draw: login, token, validation, expiry, refresh.

Configuration and Options
What this primarily describes: Configuration is environment-specific application setup; a secret is a sensitive value such as a password, token, or connection-string credential. This slide focuses on the options pattern, appsettings and database settings, environment overrides, and keeping secrets out of source control.

Definition

The same service ran in every environment because providers supplied settings externally and strongly typed options failed fast when configuration was invalid.
  • Providers: Configuration composes sources with defined precedence, such as JSON, environment variables, and command line.
  • Options: Bind related settings to typed classes and inject the appropriate options interface.
  • Validation: Validate required values and ranges at startup when invalid configuration should block deployment.
  • Secrets: Keep secrets out of source, images, logs, and client-delivered configuration; use a managed secret store.

Slide 21 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
Caching and Invalidation
What this primarily describes: Caching keeps a reusable copy of expensive data closer to the caller, like saving a frequently used report instead of rerunning its SQL every time. TTL means Time To Live, the period before a cached value expires. This slide focuses on in-memory versus distributed caches, what to cache, and how expiry or invalidation limits stale data.

Definition

Caching made reads faster but introduced a second truth, so the design began with an explicit staleness budget and invalidation plan.
  • Memory: IMemoryCache is process-local, fast, and not shared across replicas.
  • Distributed: A distributed cache shares data across instances but adds network and serialization costs.
  • Invalidation: Bound staleness with expiration, versioned keys, events, or explicit removal.
  • Stampede: Coalesce refreshes or add jitter so many misses do not overload the dependency.

Self rating: 1 (Expected TA: 3)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: what you cached, why, and how staleness was controlled.
  • Honest answer: I did not implement Redis or IMemoryCache caching layer in my stories.
  • For clinical schedule/patient screens, we prefer fresh API read after save to avoid stale data.
  • Site config may be read once per request path — not long TTL (Time to Live) cache.
  • Self rating 1 — I understand cache tradeoffs but have no distributed cache implementation to describe.

Previous-project depth (if asked)

  • In my previous project product catalog APIs used IMemoryCache on a single server.
  • Cached: category list and price lookup keys; TTL (Time to Live) about 5–10 minutes.
  • Invalidation: on admin save, remove cache key (or short TTL if event miss).
  • Why not Redis then: one app server; later we moved shared cache to Redis when we scaled out.
  • Result: fewer DB hits on read-heavy catalog pages with bounded staleness.

Slide 22 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
Reliable Background Work
What this primarily describes: Background work runs outside the HTTP request that accepted or triggered it — like placing a long report in a job queue and returning immediately. This slide focuses on hosted services, scheduled jobs, and queues, including retries, durability, and what happens when a worker fails partway through.

Definition

A fire-and-forget request task vanished during deployment; durable work moved to a queue and a hosted consumer owned retries and shutdown.
  • BackgroundService: Runs application-managed work with a cancellation token tied to host shutdown.
  • Queue: Separates request latency from work and makes capacity, persistence, and retry semantics explicit.
  • Failure: Use idempotency, bounded retries, poison handling, and durable checkpoints as required.
  • Shutdown: Stop accepting work, signal cancellation, and drain or persist safely within the shutdown budget.

My project story (from MyDotnet.md)

My project (D22): Background work: IHostedService / queues

How: Azure Elastic Jobs / scheduled SQL for Financial Cap reset; Azure Functions for integration service/payment provider calls. Less in-proc BackgroundService ownership.

Why: Multi-tenant annual cap reset belongs in scheduled job, not web request.

-- Elastic Job FinancialCapReset2026East updates cap tables off request thread

Self rating: 2 (Expected TA: 3)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: what happens when a background task fails mid-way.
  • Financial Cap reset runs in Azure Elastic Jobs, not inside user HTTP request.
  • If job fails partway, platform retry and logging apply; SQL updates use transactions where possible.
  • On-site alternate path uses ADI file for cap update.
  • Azure Functions retry integration failures; receiver logs error without crashing host.
  • Gap: limited custom IHostedService/BackgroundService code written by me.

Previous-project depth (if asked)

  • In my previous project I implemented BackgroundService to process email/notification queue items.
  • On failure mid-way: try/catch per item, log, leave failed item for retry; do not stop the whole hosted service.
  • On graceful shutdown: CancellationToken stops loop; in-flight item finishes or is retried next start.
  • Why BackgroundService: work must continue even when no HTTP request is open.
  • Result: reliable background processing with clear failure isolation.

Slide 23 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
Layered .NET Testing
What this primarily describes: The testing pyramid recommends many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a small number of broad end-to-end tests. A unit test checks one piece in isolation; an integration test checks pieces working together. This slide focuses on xUnit, mocks, WebApplicationFactory, and choosing the correct layer for each behavior.

Definition

A controller unit test passed while routing and serialization were broken, so one integration test exercised the application through its real HTTP boundary.
  • Unit: Test deterministic business behavior quickly with minimal infrastructure.
  • Double: Mock external boundaries or nondeterminism, not every internal collaborator.
  • Integration: Test components that must agree: routing, DI, middleware, persistence, and serialization.
  • Factory: WebApplicationFactory hosts an ASP.NET Core app for realistic HTTP integration tests.

Slide 24 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
Logs Metrics and Traces
What this primarily describes: Observability means understanding a running system from its outputs: logs explain events, metrics show numeric trends, and traces follow a request across operations. This slide focuses on structured logging, metrics, distributed traces, and health checks so production problems can be triaged by site and operation.

Definition

A single correlation ID connected a slow request's trace, dependency span, and structured error log, turning an alert into an explanation.
  • Logs: Use structured properties and scopes; avoid secrets and uncontrolled high-cardinality fields.
  • Metrics: Track rates, errors, duration, saturation, and business signals suitable for dashboards and alerts.
  • Traces: Propagate context across services and dependencies to explain individual request paths.
  • Health: Separate liveness from readiness and keep checks cheap and meaningful.

Slide 25 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
Reliable Message Consumers
What this primarily describes: Messaging lets systems exchange work asynchronously through a queue or bus, like an inbox that preserves messages until a consumer handles them. A DLQ is a Dead-Letter Queue for messages that repeatedly fail. This slide focuses on consumers, retries, DLQs, and idempotent processing so duplicate delivery does not duplicate effects.

Definition

A consumer processed the same payment twice after crashing before acknowledgement, proving that at-least-once delivery requires idempotent effects.
  • Ack: Acknowledge only after required processing succeeds; understand each broker's delivery semantics.
  • Retry: Retry transient failures with limits and backoff, not permanent validation failures.
  • DLQ: Quarantine poison messages with reason, context, alerts, and a replay procedure.
  • Idempotency: Use stable message IDs, deduplication records, or naturally idempotent writes.

Slide 26 of 72 · D2 — ASP.NET & Web
Hosting and Scaling
What this primarily describes: Hosting is where and how an application process runs; deployment is how a built version reaches that environment. Kestrel is ASP.NET Core's web server, IIS is Microsoft's Internet Information Services host/proxy, and containers package an app with its runtime. This slide focuses on topology and what must change when the app scales to multiple instances.

Definition

Adding replicas improved throughput only after session state and file storage stopped living inside one process.
  • Kestrel: The cross-platform ASP.NET Core web server handles application HTTP traffic.
  • Proxy: IIS or another reverse proxy can terminate TLS, apply edge policy, and forward to Kestrel.
  • Container: Package immutable application artifacts with explicit configuration, limits, and health probes.
  • Scale: Scale stateless replicas from measured CPU, latency, concurrency, or queue pressure.

Slide 27 of 72 · D3 — Data & SQL
SQL Joins and Windows
What this primarily describes: SQL means Structured Query Language — the language used to retrieve and change relational data. Joins combine related tables, GROUP BY summarizes rows, and window functions calculate across related rows without collapsing them. This slide focuses on selecting the right form for common querying and reporting needs.

Definition

A sales report joined customers, orders, and lines, then used a window function to rank totals without collapsing each row's context.
  • Join: Choose join type from required row preservation and join on explicit relational keys.
  • GROUP BY: Collapses rows into groups; every selected nonaggregate must belong to the grouping.
  • Window: Computes across a partition while retaining individual rows.
  • Grain: State the intended row grain before joining to avoid accidental multiplication.

Composite Index Design
What this primarily describes: A database index is an ordered lookup structure, like a book index that avoids scanning every page. A composite index contains more than one column, and its order affects which searches it can serve efficiently. This slide focuses on faster reads, column order, covering queries, and the extra storage and write cost of indexes.

Definition

An index on (TenantId, CreatedAt) transformed a tenant timeline query because its leading column matched the equality predicate and its suffix supported range ordering.
  • Index: An index trades storage and write work for faster qualifying reads.
  • Order: Composite column order should reflect equality, range, sorting, selectivity, and engine behavior.
  • Covering: Included columns may avoid base-table lookups but increase index size and maintenance.
  • Cost: Every insert, update, and delete may maintain indexes; unused overlap hurts write throughput.

Reading Query Plans
What this primarily describes: A query execution plan is the database engine's chosen recipe for running SQL, showing operations such as scans, seeks, joins, and sorts. This slide focuses on reading estimated costs and actual row counts, finding the reason for slow SQL, and comparing the plan before and after a measured fix.

Definition

The slow query was not fixed by guessing an index; its plan showed a cardinality error that drove an expensive join strategy.
  • Plan: Read operators, data flow, join algorithms, predicates, sorts, and memory behavior.
  • Estimate: Large estimated-versus-actual row gaps can indicate stale statistics or correlated predicates.
  • Access: A scan is not automatically bad and a seek is not automatically good; cost depends on rows and lookups.
  • Compare: Capture duration, reads, rows, and plan before and after one controlled change.

Slide 30 of 72 · D3 — Data & SQL
Transactions Locks Deadlocks
What this primarily describes: A transaction groups database changes so they succeed or fail as one unit, like a bank transfer that must both debit and credit. Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe, while locks protect changing data. This slide focuses on consistent multi-table writes and avoiding long locks and deadlocks.

Definition

Two valid requests oversold the last unit because each read availability before either committed; correctness required one atomic concurrency strategy.
  • Transaction: Groups operations into an atomic consistency boundary with commit or rollback.
  • Isolation: Controls which concurrent effects are visible and which anomalies are prevented.
  • Lock: Locks protect resources but can block; scope and access order shape contention.
  • Deadlock: A cycle of waits causes one transaction to be chosen as victim; retry and remove the cycle's cause.

Slide 31 of 72 · D3 — Data & SQL
Schema Design Tradeoffs
What this primarily describes: A database schema defines how data is organized and related. Normalization separates facts to reduce duplication; denormalization repeats or pre-combines data to make reads simpler or faster. OLTP means Online Transaction Processing. This slide focuses on integrity for transactional systems versus reporting speed and document-shaped reads.

Definition

The write model stored each fact once, while a deliberate read model duplicated display data to serve a high-volume query cheaply.
  • Normalize: Separate facts to reduce update anomalies and express relationships clearly.
  • Denormalize: Duplicate or precompute data for a measured read need with an explicit synchronization owner.
  • Constraint: Use keys, foreign keys, uniqueness, and checks to preserve invariants where the database can enforce them.
  • Tradeoff: Evaluate read shape, write rate, consistency tolerance, storage, and operational complexity.

Slide 32 of 72 · D3 — Data & SQL
ORM or Native SQL
What this primarily describes: An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) maps application objects to relational tables, while native SQL and SPs (stored procedures) express database work directly. It is like choosing a translator for routine conversations but speaking SQL directly for specialized work. This slide focuses on that choice and on batching set-based operations at high volume.

Definition

The ORM was ideal for ordinary updates, but a million-row reconciliation needed a set-based statement instead of a million tracked entities.
  • ORM: Provides mapping, composable queries, change tracking, and maintainable common data access.
  • SQL: Use native SQL when a provider cannot express or efficiently execute a proven critical operation.
  • Batch: Prefer set-based updates, bulk APIs, staging tables, or bounded batches at volume.
  • Safety: Parameterize SQL, preserve transactions and observability, and isolate database-specific code.

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: where you bypassed ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) and what benefit you got.
  • Entire API Data Access uses ADO.NET + stored procedures — no Entity Framework ORM.
  • Benefit: predictable SQL plans, DBA-owned scripts, easy multi-tenant filters inside SPs (Stored Procedures).
  • Cost: manual mapping from SqlDataReader to DTO (Data Transfer Object) classes.
  • High-volume Financial Cap update uses set-based Elastic Job, not row-by-row API updates.
  • Result: better control and performance for healthcare SQL workloads.

Previous-project depth (if asked)

  • In my previous EF Core (Entity Framework Core) project, most CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) used EF, but a month-end report bypassed ORM (Object-Relational Mapper).
  • Why bypass: complex joins + large aggregation were slow and hard to tune through LINQ.
  • We called a stored procedure / raw SQL for that report only; EF stayed for normal screens.
  • Benefit: DBA (Database Administrator) could tune the SP (Stored Procedure) plan; app stayed simple for CRUD.
  • Result: hybrid approach — ORM for productivity, native SQL where volume/complexity needed it.

Slide 33 of 72 · D3 — Data & SQL
Connection Pool Sizing
What this primarily describes: Connection pooling keeps reusable database connections instead of paying to open a new one for every command — like returning a tool to a shared toolbox. This slide focuses on opening late, closing early, and preventing pool exhaustion caused by leaks or by holding connections during slow HTTP calls.

Definition

Requests timed out while the database looked idle because all pooled connections were waiting inside long transactions.
  • Pool: Reuses physical connections; logical open and close usually borrow and return a pooled connection.
  • Exhaustion: Appears as acquisition waits or timeouts, often caused by leaks, slow queries, long transactions, or excess concurrency.
  • Size: Size from database capacity, replica count, workload concurrency, and connection hold time.
  • Disposal: Open late, close early, and always dispose connections, commands, and readers.

My project (D33): Connection pooling

How: Rely on ADO.NET pooling; leaks (undisposed connections) showed as timeouts under load. Fix dispose; don’t open connection per tiny field update in loops.

using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs); // return to pool on dispose

Self rating: 2 (Expected TA: 3)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: connection pool exhaustion symptoms and how you tuned.
  • Symptom: random SQL timeout expired errors for many sites sharing same IIS (Internet Information Services) app pool.
  • Root cause: leaked connections from undisposed SqlDataReader — not Max Pool Size too small.
  • Fix: using/dispose pattern; close reader after mapping; never keep SQL open during external HTTP call.
  • We raised Max Pool Size only after confirming leaks were fixed.
  • Result: timeouts stopped after DA (Data Access) dispose corrections.

Slide 34 of 72 · D3 — Data & SQL
Choosing NoSQL Models
What this primarily describes: SQL databases organize related data in tables with schemas, joins, and strong transactions; NoSQL means Not Only SQL and includes document, key-value, and other models optimized for different access patterns. This slide focuses on choosing from requirements such as relationships, transactions, flexible documents, and scale.

Definition

A session lookup needed one key and short-lived value, while financial posting needed relational constraints and transactions; the access pattern chose the store.
  • Document: Fits aggregate-shaped records retrieved and updated mainly as a unit.
  • Key-value: Fits direct key lookup, caching, sessions, counters, and simple value access.
  • Columnar: Column-family or analytical columnar systems serve different large-scale sparse or scan-heavy patterns.
  • Consistency: Choose consistency guarantees from business invariants, conflict behavior, and latency needs.

Slide 35 of 72 · D3 — Data & SQL
Team Schema Migrations
What this primarily describes: A schema migration is a versioned change to database structure or data, similar to a code change that must be applied in the correct order everywhere. This slide focuses on reviewed migration scripts, coordination with application deployment, backward compatibility, and a tested rollback or roll-forward plan.

Definition

A zero-downtime rename used two releases: first expand the schema and support both forms, then contract only after old code disappeared.
  • Version: Store ordered migration scripts or metadata in source control and apply each version once.
  • Review: Review locking, duration, data movement, compatibility, and rollback before production.
  • Expand-contract: Add compatible structures first, backfill, switch readers and writers, then remove old structures.
  • Rollback: For destructive or data-changing migrations, forward-fix or restore may be safer than down scripts.

Slide 36 of 72 · D3 — Data & SQL
Large Data Result Patterns
What this primarily describes: Large-result handling means processing data in bounded pieces instead of loading every row into memory at once — like reading a book page by page. OOM means Out Of Memory. This slide focuses on pagination, streaming, filtering, and archival so APIs remain responsive and do not run out of memory.

Definition

An export endpoint stopped exhausting memory when it streamed bounded batches and stopped materializing the entire result before sending the first byte.
  • Pagination: Prefer stable keyset pagination for deep, changing datasets when offset cost or drift matters.
  • Streaming: Read and write incrementally while keeping connections, cancellation, and partial failure explicit.
  • Bounded: Limit page size and in-flight buffers so slow clients apply backpressure instead of growing memory.
  • Archive: Move cold data under retention and retrieval policies while preserving compliance and query needs.

  • Result: large datasets without OOM (Out Of Memory) on API servers.

Slide 37 of 72 · D4 — Engineering Craft
Algorithms Under Time Pressure
What this primarily describes: Data structures organize values for particular operations, while algorithmic complexity describes how time or memory grows as input grows. For example, a dictionary uses hashing for an average O(1) lookup, while scanning a list is O(n). This slide focuses on arrays, dictionaries, hashing, and replacing avoidable nested scans with suitable structures.

Definition

A strong candidate turns an ambiguous data problem into a clear algorithm, then explains why its time and space costs fit.
  • Clarify: confirm input shape, constraints, and expected output.
  • Choose: match the access pattern to an array, set, stack, queue, or hash map.
  • Analyze: state average and worst-case time and space complexity.
  • Prove: test empty, duplicate, boundary, and representative inputs.

My project story (from MyDotnet.md)

My project (D37): Data structures & algorithms fluency

How: Dictionaries for lookups (EpisodeId → outcomes, PatId → profile), HashSets for race/ethnicity code validation, list filters for schedule.

Why: O(1) lookup beats nested loops when linking outcomes episodes or validating USCDI codes.

var byEpisode = episodes.ToDictionary(e => e.EpisodeId); if (!byEpisode.ContainsKey(id)) return; // style guard

Self rating: 3 (Expected TA: 3)

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: solve medium problem and state complexity.
  • Problem: outcomes EpisodeId linking used nested loops — slow when list grew.
  • Solution: Dictionary<EpisodeId, episode> for O(1) average lookup; HashSet for allowed USCDI codes.
  • Complexity: nested loops O(n×m) changed to O(n) build + O(1) lookups.
  • Guard clause: if (!byEpisode.ContainsKey(id)) return; stops bad link early.
  • Result: faster validation and linking on larger datasets.

Think Aloud Live Coding
What this primarily describes: Live coding means solving a programming problem while another person watches your reasoning and implementation, so communication matters as much as the final syntax. This slide focuses on clarifying inputs, explaining a small plan, implementing incrementally, and testing edge cases before declaring the work complete.

Definition

In live coding, the interviewer evaluates the reasoning journey as much as the final C# solution.
  • Frame: restate the task and ask focused questions.
  • Plan: name the algorithm and data structures before typing.
  • Narrate: explain decisions without describing every keystroke.
  • Verify: trace examples and correct defects openly.

Slide 39 of 72 · D4 — Engineering Craft
Prove the Bug Fix
What this primarily describes: Debugging is the evidence-based process of finding why observed behavior differs from expected behavior, like narrowing a failed SQL result from query to data to parameter. This slide focuses on reproduce → isolate → fix → prove, avoiding unrelated shotgun changes.

Definition

A difficult bug becomes manageable when each observation narrows the fault until one testable cause remains.
  • Reproduce: capture inputs, environment, timing, and symptoms.
  • Isolate: compare healthy and failing paths and change one variable at a time.
  • Fix: correct the root cause rather than masking the symptom.
  • Prove: add a regression test and verify production signals.

My project (D39): Debugging methodology

How: Hard bug: SignalR Core migration — old null group check invalid; isolated by comparing OWIN vs Core behavior, then repro with empty group, then SendAsync no-op solution; proved with web client multi-tab test.

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: hard bug story — reproduce, isolate, fix, prove.
  • Bug: realtime notifications stopped working after Framework to Core API migration.
  • Reproduce: open two web client tabs; save appointment in one; other tab did not update.
  • Isolate: tested middleware token, hub send, and client handler separately.
  • Root cause: old Framework pattern (check if group is null) does not apply in Core — SendAsync to empty group is safe.
  • Fix: always SendAsync; refresh client data on reconnect.
  • Prove: repeated multi-tab test and shared documentation with team.

Q: Where did you use Prove the Bug Fix in your project?

A: Hard bug: SignalR Core migration — old null group check invalid; isolated by comparing OWIN vs Core behavior, then repro with empty group, then SendAsync no-op solution; proved with web client multi-tab test. Structured isolate prevents shotgun changes across proxy + hub + client.

Q: Explain Prove the Bug Fix for an interviewer.

A: I describe the first reliable reproduction, the competing hypotheses, and the experiment that eliminated each one. I finish with the regression test and production evidence that proved both recovery and prevention.

Q: What does Level-3 look like for this skill?

A: Tells a hard-bug story with the actual isolation steps, not just the fix

Q: Give your assessor talking points.

A: Level-3 asks: hard bug story — reproduce, isolate, fix, prove. Bug: realtime notifications stopped working after Framework to Core API migration. Reproduce: open two web client tabs; save appointment in one; other tab did not update. Isolate: tested middleware token, hub send, and client handler separately.

Change Unfamiliar Code Safely
What this primarily describes: A safe change improves unfamiliar code while limiting the blast radius — the amount of the system that could be affected if the assumption is wrong. This slide focuses on understanding ownership and call paths, preserving behavior with tests, and making small reversible changes.

Definition

When ownership history is missing, tests and runtime evidence become the map for a safe change.
  • Map: trace entry points, dependencies, data flow, and callers.
  • Characterize: lock current behavior with focused tests.
  • Limit: keep the diff small and identify affected consumers.
  • Observe: release gradually and watch relevant signals.

Reviews That Improve Design
What this primarily describes: Git records versioned code history, while code review lets teammates examine a proposed change before it is merged. A PR means Pull Request, the reviewable package of commits. This slide focuses on small meaningful PRs and feedback about correctness, design, tests, and maintainability rather than style alone.

Definition

A valuable review protects correctness and maintainability while helping the author improve the design.
  • Prepare: keep commits focused and explain intent and test evidence.
  • Review: prioritize correctness, contracts, security, and operability.
  • Communicate: label blockers, suggestions, and questions clearly.
  • Respond: test feedback objectively and document the outcome.

Refactor Without Missing Deadlines
What this primarily describes: Refactoring changes code structure without intentionally changing its behavior. A strangler approach replaces an old system piece by piece while a proxy routes between old and new. This slide focuses on tests, incremental delivery, and reversible steps that reduce the risk of a big-bang rewrite.

Definition

Under deadline pressure, disciplined refactoring creates a narrow safe path instead of a risky rewrite.
  • Target: tie the refactor to a concrete delivery or reliability need.
  • Protect: add tests around behavior before moving structure.
  • Slice: use small, independently releasable steps.
  • Measure: confirm behavior, performance, and defect rates remain healthy.

Build Trustworthy Delivery Pipelines
What this primarily describes: CI/CD means Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment — code changes are automatically built, tested, and prepared or released through a repeatable pipeline. This slide focuses on stages, quality gates, artifact promotion, and stopping an unsafe change before it reaches production.

Definition

A delivery pipeline turns every commit into repeatable evidence that the same artifact is safe to release.
  • Build: compile once and create an immutable versioned artifact.
  • Verify: run tests, security scans, and policy checks.
  • Promote: move the same artifact through environments.
  • Release: use approvals, health checks, and rollback automation.

Slide 44 of 72 · D4 — Engineering Craft
Lead Production Incident Recovery
What this primarily describes: A production incident is an unplanned service disruption or degradation affecting real users. Incident handling is like emergency response: stabilize first, investigate with evidence, then prevent recurrence. This slide focuses on detection, triage with logs/metrics/traces, mitigation, root-cause analysis, and follow-up actions.

Definition

During an incident, restore service first, preserve evidence, and turn the timeline into prevention afterward.
  • Detect: confirm user impact and establish severity.
  • Correlate: connect metrics, structured logs, traces, and recent changes.
  • Mitigate: roll back, disable, scale, or degrade safely.
  • Prevent: fix the cause and improve detection and runbooks.

Slide 45 of 72 · D5 — Architecture
Design Durable API Contracts
What this primarily describes: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a contract clients use to communicate with a service. Idempotency means safely repeating the same request without creating extra effects, like setting a value twice rather than adding twice. This slide focuses on idempotency, pagination, versioning, and stable error contracts that do not break consumers.

Definition

An API is a long-lived promise: retries, growth, errors, and client evolution must be designed before production exposes them.
  • Retry safely: use idempotency keys for repeatable writes.
  • Bound reads: paginate stable ordered collections.
  • Evolve: prefer additive changes and version breaking contracts deliberately.
  • Standardize: return machine-readable error codes and trace identifiers.

Slide 46 of 72 · D5 — Architecture
Draw Boundaries That Last
What this primarily describes: Service layers and boundaries divide responsibilities so each part has a clear job, like a controller receiving an order and a data-access layer storing it. DA means Data Access. This slide focuses on the flow from Controllers → DA → SQL or external integrations, with controlled dependency direction and clear ownership.

Definition

A maintainable service keeps business decisions inward and replaceable infrastructure details at the edges.
  • API: translate transport concerns into application requests.
  • Application: coordinate use cases and transaction boundaries.
  • Domain: own business rules without infrastructure dependencies.
  • Infrastructure: implement persistence and external adapters.
