Slide 47 of 72 · D5 — Architecture
Scale Stateless Services Horizontally
What this primarily describes: A distributed system spreads work across multiple processes or machines. A stateless API can handle any request on any instance, while stateful features remember client-specific information. This slide focuses on scaling out stateless APIs and supporting sessions or SignalR with sticky routing or a shared backplane.

Definition

Horizontal scaling works when any healthy instance can handle the next request without hidden local state.
  • Externalize: keep durable session and workflow state in shared systems.
  • Balance: route traffic only to healthy instances.
  • Scale: add instances using demand and saturation signals.
  • Constrain: account for database, connection, and dependency limits.

Slide 48 of 72 · D5 — Architecture
Cache Without Serving Surprises
What this primarily describes: Caching architecture decides where reusable copies live — for example in a browser, application instance, or distributed cache — and how they stay acceptably fresh. TTL means Time To Live. This slide focuses on cache layers, expiry versus event-driven invalidation, and explicitly bounding stale reads.

Definition

A cache is a deliberate consistency trade: every fast read needs an explicit freshness and failure policy.
  • Select: cache expensive, frequent, reusable reads.
  • Expire: choose TTL from acceptable staleness and update frequency.
  • Invalidate: use events when important changes must propagate quickly.
  • Protect: handle misses, stampedes, and cache outages.

Slide 49 of 72 · D5 — Architecture
Make Messaging Fail Safely
What this primarily describes: Asynchronous messaging lets a sender publish work without waiting for the receiver to finish; queues distribute work, while publish/subscribe broadcasts events to subscribers. DLQ means Dead-Letter Queue, where repeatedly failed messages are isolated. This slide focuses on retries, idempotency, delivery guarantees, and failed-consumer handling.

Definition

Reliable messaging assumes duplicates, delays, reordering, and poison messages are normal operating conditions.
  • Choose: use a queue for work distribution and pub/sub for independent reactions.
  • Retry: back off transient failures with a strict attempt limit.
  • Deduplicate: make consumers idempotent using stable message identity.
  • Quarantine: send persistent failures to a monitored DLQ.

Slide 50 of 72 · D5 — Architecture
Contain Failures by Design
What this primarily describes: Resilience is a system's ability to keep serving useful results when a dependency is slow or unavailable. A circuit breaker stops repeated calls to a failing service, while a bulkhead isolates failures like compartments in a ship. This slide focuses on timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and graceful degradation.

Definition

Resilience is not retrying everything; it is bounding damage and preserving the most valuable service behavior.
  • Timeout: stop waiting before the caller's budget expires.
  • Break: pause calls to a dependency that is predictably failing.
  • Isolate: reserve concurrency so one dependency cannot exhaust all capacity.
  • Degrade: return a safe reduced experience when possible.

Excel / assessor talking points

  • Level-3 asks: failure modes your service survives and how each is handled.

Previous-project depth (if asked)

  • In my previous project we wrapped vendor HttpClient with Polly: timeout, retry, circuit breaker.
  • Failure mode: vendor outage opened circuit after N failures → API returned friendly "temporarily unavailable".
  • Bulkhead idea: limit concurrent vendor calls so one slow vendor cannot consume all threads.
  • After interval, circuit half-open tested one call then closed if healthy.
  • Result: our core APIs stayed up during vendor downtime.

Slide 51 of 72 · D5 — Architecture
Turn NFRs Into Numbers
What this primarily describes: NFR means Non-Functional Requirement — a measurable quality target describing how well a system must operate, rather than which feature it performs. Examples include latency, availability, throughput, security, and recovery time. This slide focuses on stating NFRs as numbers and defining how tests and monitoring will verify them.

Definition

A non-functional requirement becomes actionable only when it names a signal, target, scope, and measurement window.
  • Availability: define successful eligible requests over a time window.
  • Latency: use percentiles, not averages, for user experience.
  • Throughput: state sustained and peak load expectations.
  • Verify: combine production telemetry with representative load tests.

Slide 52 of 72 · D5 — Architecture
Estimate Capacity Before Scaling
What this primarily describes: Capacity planning estimates how much traffic and data a system can handle before a resource becomes a bottleneck. RPS means Requests Per Second, a common traffic rate. This slide focuses on converting users into RPS and resource demand, estimating instance count, and identifying the real constraint, which is often SQL.

Definition

A useful capacity estimate makes assumptions visible, converts demand into load, and checks every constrained dependency.
  • Demand: estimate active users and actions per interval.
  • Peak: apply a measured or explicit peak-to-average factor.
  • Supply: use tested safe throughput per instance.
  • Headroom: include failures, growth, and downstream limits.

Slide 53 of 72 · D5 — Architecture
Map Threats to Controls
What this primarily describes: Security architecture builds protections into system boundaries, data flows, and defaults. OWASP means Open Worldwide Application Security Project, which publishes practical guidance on common application risks. This slide focuses on mapping controls to injection, broken authentication/authorization, secret exposure, and unsafe error messages.

Definition

Security architecture connects concrete threats in a real request path to preventive, detective, and recovery controls.
  • Authorize: enforce object and action permissions server-side.
  • Validate: use parameterized access and constrained input handling.
  • Protect: encrypt sensitive data and minimize its retention.
  • Manage: store secrets in a vault, rotate them, and avoid logs.

Q: Where did you use Map Threats to Controls in your project?

A: JWT auth, `[Authorize]`, CORS allowlist for SignalR, PCI via hosted TokenPay/payment gateway iframes (no raw PAN in our API), parameterized SQL (no string-concat), secrets out of source. PHI/payment data — injection, XSS, broken auth are high risk.

Q: Explain Map Threats to Controls for an interviewer.

A: In our project, broken access control was mitigated with resource-level authorization, injection with parameterized queries, and security misconfiguration with hardened deployment templates and automated scans. Secrets came from managed identity and a vault, while sensitive fields were encrypted and redacted from logs.

Q: What does Level-3 look like for this skill?

A: Maps 3+ OWASP risks to concrete mitigations in their own project

Q: Give your assessor talking points.

A: Level-3 asks: map 3+ OWASP risks to concrete project mitigations. Injection: always SqlParameter and stored procedures — never concatenate user input into SQL. Broken authentication: JWT (JSON Web Token) bearer + [Authorize] on protected API controllers. Sensitive data exposure: payment uses hosted iframe — card number never stored in our API; secrets only in Azure config.

Definition

  • Trace: follow sampled requests across service boundaries.
  • Alert: page on actionable symptoms tied to user impact.

Slide 55 of 72 · D5 — Architecture
Explain Architecture Tradeoffs Clearly
What this primarily describes: A tradeoff is an intentional exchange: gaining one quality usually costs another, such as stronger consistency adding latency. This slide focuses on explaining decisions clearly as "we accepted X to gain Y," using evidence about cost, performance, reliability, and migration risk.

Definition

A credible architecture decision names the constraint, alternatives, benefit gained, cost accepted, and trigger to revisit.
  • Frame: state the decision and the dominant constraint.
  • Compare: evaluate realistic alternatives using the same criteria.
  • Accept: make the downside and mitigation explicit.
  • Adapt: explain what changed constraint would reverse the choice.

1. STAR structure — full example

What it means: interviewers want ownership and decisions, not a ticket dump.

❌ Before
// BEFORE — vague team story We migrated SignalR and fixed some issues. The team worked on adapters.
✔ After
// AFTER — STAR with “I” S: jQuery SignalR ≠ Core SignalR protocol. T: I owned a design that keeps v14 + v15 clients live. A: I proposed 3 solutions; detailed Solution3 bridge. R: Design accepted; I implemented the adapters.
How to tell it in 2 minutes
  1. Situation: one sentence on the incompatibility (legacy jQuery client → TASNX Core hub).
  2. Task: “I took ownership beyond my original ticket because this blocked the epic.”
  3. Action: name Solution1/2/3 briefly, then zoom into the bridge you designed.
  4. Result: recognition + follow-on adapter work + legacy + new clients both get updates.

2. Story A — SignalR ownership

Why it matters in my project: this was the main purpose of the migration epic — realtime for schedule/accounting.

STARWhat I say
SLegacy jQuery SignalR clients could not connect to migrated TASNX (.NET Core / .NET 10 SignalR) — incompatible protocol.
TI went beyond my assigned ticket, researched options, and proposed architecture so both client generations keep working.
ASolution1: migrate WinForm clients to Microsoft SignalR (ideal, but clients must upgrade).

1. Accountability — full example

What it means: say the gap in one sentence without blaming another team.

❌ Before
// BEFORE — blame / vague SignalR was confusing because Core is different. Someone should have documented it.
✔ After
// AFTER — own the gap I assumed Framework null-check patterns must be copied. I was wrong — I should have verified Core semantics first.

2. Challenge — SignalR dynamic → strongly typed (no group existence check)

Problem: OWIN used dynamic client methods and checked if the group was null. ASP.NET Core SignalR has no “does this group have clients?” API.

❌ Before
// OLD (OWIN) — pattern does not exist in Core dynamic group = _hub.Clients.Group(siteName, new string[0]); if (group == null) { return; } group.AccountingBatchUpdated(json);
✔ After
// SOLUTION — empty group SendAsync is a safe no-op await _hubContext.Clients.Group(siteName.ToLower()) .SendAsync("AccountingBatchUpdated", json); // No clients connected → silently ignored (desired)
BeatWhat happened
GapI treated Framework/OWIN SignalR patterns as drop-in for Core.
ImpactExtra time / confusion on realtime notifications after migration.
ResponseReproduced multi-tab case; learned Core empty-group send is safe; fixed + documented.
PreventionFramework-diff checklist before porting; ask owners before overlapping fixes.

3. Challenge — JsonElement conversion failures in the proxy

Problem: When legacy TAS proxied to TASNX, System.Text.Json left integers as JsonElement. SqlParameter could not convert JsonElement → Int32 (“Failed to convert parameter from JsonElement to Int32”).

❌ Before
// BEFORE — System.Text.Json wraps values as JsonElement // SqlParameter fails: JsonElement → Int32 services.AddControllers(); // default STJ
✔ After
// SOLUTION — Newtonsoft deserializes to native types services.AddControllers() .AddNewtonsoftJson(opt => { opt.SerializerSettings.ContractResolver = new DefaultContractResolver(); // PascalCase }); // Also trim Content-Type in proxy middleware: var mediaType = contentType.Split(';')[0].Trim(); // application/json; charset=utf-8 → application/json

4. Challenge — tautological unit tests (false confidence)

Problem: tests that can never fail look green but prove nothing. Assert.NotNull(success.ToString()) is meaningless — bool.ToString() always returns "True"/"False", never null. Suite also lacked failure paths.

❌ Before
// BEFORE — can NEVER fail Assert.NotNull(success.ToString()); // only success-path setups
✔ After
// AFTER — meaningful assert + failure path Assert.IsType<bool>(success); _mock.Setup(x => x.SendAsync(It.IsAny<string>())) .ReturnsAsync(false); // simulate queue failure Assert.False(await _mock.Object.SendAsync("test"));

5. Challenge — StringValues API (.Length vs .Count)

Problem: SignalR middleware used originHeader.Length — that API does not exist on StringValues. Also null-checked a struct (structs are never null).

❌ Before
// WRONG — StringValues is a struct; has .Count not .Length if (bearer != null && bearer.Length > 0) // compile error
✔ After
// FIXED — use .Count; drop null check if (bearer.Count > 0) // OK

6. Challenge — Bluefin payment (WCF) — fix was the DLL, not the code

Problem: After migration, one Bluefin payment-gateway path that used WCF threw WCF errors. AI tools and web search did not help — suggestions kept looping on the same code-level “fixes.”

❌ Before
// BEFORE — stuck in AI / Google loop // Same code suggestions repeated; still fails // Assumption: “must change WCF client code”
✔ After
// SOLUTION — isolate with a POC // 1) New .NET Framework 4.8 project + Bluefin gateway // 2) Migrate that POC to .NET 8 — works // Root cause: different DLL version in the real app // Fix: align the DLL — not rewrite payment code
BeatWhat I say
StuckWCF error on Bluefin after migrate; AI kept proposing the same code changes.
MethodMinimal POC: Framework 4.8 + gateway → migrate POC to .NET 8.
ResultPOC worked → proved app config/DLL mismatch, not business logic.
LessonWhen tools loop, stop chatting — isolate. Sometimes the fix is the assembly version.

  2. Concrete recovery (repro → root cause → code or DLL fix → prove).

❌ Before

✔ After

❌ Before

OptionIdeaWhy it lost / tradeoff

1. Criteria — full example

What good criteria looked like:

  • Keep legacy UI unchanged (v14.1.44.0).
  • Let new clients use modern SignalR on TASNX.
  • Prefer one place to fix API bugs (TASNX).
  • Allow a quick test path, then sunset TAS later.

2. Why Solution3 (bridge) — before/after thinking

❌ Before
// BEFORE — pick dual APIs without tradeoff talk Just keep TAS and TASNX both implementing features. // Hidden cost: every fix twice
✔ After
// AFTER — explicit tradeoff Bridge: ForwardMiddleware → TASNX for /api/* TASNX → LegacySignalRController → jQuery hub Advantage: fix APIs only in TASNX; legacy SignalR unchanged
How the bridge decision works
  1. Legacy client posts appointment to TAS /api/....
  2. ForwardMiddleware forwards method/path/body to TASNX (skips /signalr*).
  3. TASNX processes, returns HTTP result, broadcasts Core SignalR to new clients.
  4. TASNX POSTs to TAS /api/LegacySignalR/Notify so jQuery hub reaches v14 clients.

3. Other decisions (keep ready)

  • ADO.NET/SPs vs introducing EF mid-migration — risk/time.
  • Cosmos for Registry admin config vs wide SQL tables — flexible reporting fields.
  • Dual-stack proxy vs big-bang rewrite — clinic uptime.

OOP Principles Pack
What this primarily describes: OOP here is a scenario pack, not four dictionary definitions. Interviewers name one keyword (interface vs abstract, sealed, record, var vs dynamic) and expects where it showed up in TAS/TASNX or a similar service.

Definition

Interviewers pick one OOP keyword and expect a project scenario, not a textbook list. Start from the problem, then name the language tool that solved it.
  • Abstraction: Hide how work is done behind a stable contract (interface or abstract API) so callers do not depend on a concrete class.
  • Encapsulation: Keep invalid states impossible by making fields private and exposing controlled methods.
  • Interface vs abstract: Interface = capability you can mix; abstract class = shared base with optional implementation. Prefer interface when multiple unrelated types share a behavior.
  • Abstract vs virtual: Abstract must be overridden; virtual may be overridden. Use abstract when the base has no sensible default.
  • this vs base: this is the current instance; base calls the parent implementation. Say this when explaining constructor chaining.
  • Static / sealed / private ctor: Static = type-level, no instance. Sealed = no further inheritance. Private constructor = control creation (singleton factory, static class-like).
  • Extension methods: Add methods to a type you do not own, without inheritance. Keep them discoverable and side-effect free.
  • var vs dynamic: var is compile-time inference. dynamic skips compile-time checking — avoid in APIs. Records give value-like equality for DTOs.

SOLID With a Change Story
What this primarily describes: SOLID is a change story: problem → class/interface that changed → how the next variant can be added without editing working code. OCP + DIP are the ones they probe most.

Definition

Interviewers do not accept “open for extension, closed for modification” as the whole answer. They want the problem, the class that changed, and how the next variant can be added.
  • OCP story: A new device or payment path should be a new class behind an interface, not a growing if/else in a working service.
  • DIP: High-level policy depends on abstractions. Controllers depend on IOrderService, not SqlOrderRepository.
  • LSP: A subtype must honor the base contract. Do not throw NotImplementedException in an override the caller already uses.
  • SRP / ISP: One reason to change per class; fat interfaces force unused methods. Split IReadOrders from IWriteOrders when callers differ.

Repository and Unit of Work
What this primarily describes: A repository names an intention-revealing query. A unit of work is one business commit. In EF Core, DbContext.SaveChanges already is the unit of work.

Definition

A repository hides query details behind an intention-revealing method. A unit of work is one business transaction: several changes, one commit. In EF Core, DbContext already is the unit of work.
  • Repository: IDeviceRepository.GetActiveAsync() instead of repeating Include/Where in every handler.
  • Unit of Work: One IUnitOfWork.SaveChangesAsync() after the use-case mutates several aggregates.
  • EF overlap: Do not wrap every DbSet blindly. Add a repository when the query is reused or the domain must not reference EF.
  • Without it: Handlers leak SQL-shaped queries, transactions split across methods, and tests cannot fake persistence.

CQRS — Exact Scenario
What this primarily describes: CQRS means separate write commands from read queries — possibly different models. It is not “we registered MediatR.” Be ready to say when it would be unnecessary.

Definition

CQRS means Command Query Responsibility Segregation: writes (commands that change state) and reads (queries that return data) can use different models. It is not “we have MediatR.”
  • Command: CreateOrder, DebitWallet — validate, mutate, persist, maybe publish an event.
  • Query: GetOrderList — often a flattened DTO, sometimes a different store or SQL view.
  • Why split: Write model stays transactional and strict; read model is denormalized for a screen that would otherwise join five tables.
  • When not: A CRUD module with one table and low traffic does not need CQRS. Do not claim it unless the pain was real.

Q: Explain CQRS — Exact Scenario for an interviewer.

A: I would use CQRS when the order write path needed invariants and the list page needed a denormalized projection that we could scale independently. If both sides were the same EF entities with simple filters, I would not split them.

A: Gives the exact scenario that justified separate read/write models — or says we did not need it

Saga and Compensating Actions
What this primarily describes: A saga coordinates Order → Payment → Inventory → Shipment across services. SQL rollback cannot span those databases; you publish compensating actions.

Definition

A saga coordinates a business flow across services that each have their own database. There is no single SQL transaction. If shipment fails, you compensate (refund, restock) with more events.
  • Why not one SQL transaction: Each microservice owns its DB. You cannot BEGIN TRAN across independently deployed services.
  • Happy path: OrderCreated → PaymentCaptured → InventoryReserved → Shipped.
  • Failure: If InventoryReserved fails after payment, publish PaymentRefundRequested — a compensating action.
  • Choreography vs orchestration: Choreography: each service reacts to events. Orchestration: one coordinator tells each step. Name which you used.

EF Mapping: Code First, Fluent API, SPs
What this primarily describes: Code First vs Database First, Fluent API mappings, and calling a stored procedure with FromSqlInterpolated — plus wrapping related writes in a transaction.

Definition

Code First starts from classes and migrations. Database First starts from an existing schema. Fluent API configures mappings that attributes cannot express cleanly. SPs are called explicitly, not magically.
  • Code First: Entities + migrations in source control. Good for new services you own.
  • Database First: Scaffold or maintain mappings against a legacy SQL Server schema you cannot rewrite overnight.
  • Fluent API: HasConversion, composite keys, restrict delete — keep OnModelCreating for mappings that clutter entities.
  • Stored procedures: FromSqlInterpolated / ExecuteSql for set-based work already proven in SQL. Wrap in a transaction if it must pair with other writes.

Large Payload and Object References
What this primarily describes: Large files should not hop every microservice or sit on a queue. Store the object, put a reference (key/URI/checksum) on the event, process async.

Definition

A 200 MB file should not travel API Gateway → service A → queue → service B. Store the bytes in object storage, publish a reference (bucket/key or URL), and let the consumer pull.
  • Why not on the bus: Brokers and API payloads have size limits; large messages kill retries and memory.
  • Pattern: Upload/stream to S3 (or equivalent) → persist metadata in SQL → publish {key, size, checksum}.
  • Streaming / chunking: Do not load the whole file into a byte[] on the web request if you can stream to storage.
  • Async: Return 202 + job id; the consumer processes the object off the request thread.

SSO, IdentityServer, Cognito Awareness
What this primarily describes: The API validates tokens from an identity provider (OIDC / IdentityServer / Cognito). IAM is for AWS resources (ECS task roles), not the Angular user’s password.

Definition

Authentication is usually delegated to an identity provider. The API validates tokens; it does not store passwords. Name the real IdP. Do not invent IdentityServer if the project used Cognito or Azure AD.
  • SSO: One login session used by several apps via the same IdP.
  • IdentityServer / OIDC: Issues tokens after an OAuth/OIDC flow. The API uses JWT bearer validation.
  • Cognito: AWS-managed user pools + tokens. Same idea: API trusts the issuer and audience.
  • IAM: AWS identities and policies for services (who can assume a role), not the Angular user's JWT.

Events vs REST and Event Size
What this primarily describes: REST when the user is waiting; events when others must react after a commit. Large event payloads follow the object-reference pattern.

Definition

REST is a request/response you need now (get device status). Events are for work others must react to without blocking the caller (order placed → notify, invoice, analytics).
  • REST: User is waiting; you need an immediate answer or a consistent read of your own data.
  • Events: Multiple consumers, temporal decoupling, spikes you want to buffer.
  • Failure: Timeouts and retries on REST; at-least-once + idempotency + DLQ on events.
  • Large payload: Same as D67: object store + reference on the message.

Global Exceptions and Correlation
What this primarily describes: Global exception middleware logs with a trace id and returns a stable error body. After the controller returns, middleware does run again as the pipeline unwinds.

Definition

One middleware catches unhandled exceptions, logs with a correlation / trace id, and returns a stable error contract. After the controller returns, middleware does run again on the way out (the pipeline unwinds).
  • On the way in: Request hits exception, auth, then endpoint — registration order.
  • On the way out: Yes: each middleware's code after await next() runs in reverse. That is how you add headers or time the request.
  • Contract: ProblemDetails + trace id. Never leak SQL or stack traces to Angular.
  • Angular side: Interceptor maps 401 to login and 5xx to a friendly message using the same trace id for support.
